The predatory carp Chanodichthys erythropterus is a large-bodied cyprinid native to freshwater systems of eastern Asia, attaining an ultimate total length of 103 centimeters [Li = 103 centimeters]. This species exhibits a notable size dimorphism, with females generally reaching greater lengths than males in field surveys conducted across the Amur River basin. At birth, newly emerged yolk-sac larvae possess a wet weight of only 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of approximately 1.3 millimeters, which produces an extremely small prolarva upon chorion rupture. The initial mass is consistent with the lecithotrophic strategy typical of pelagic cyprinid eggs, wherein the yolk-dependent larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first days after eclosion. This modest starting mass, less than two milligrams, imposes a high vulnerability to starvation during the window between mouth opening and the onset of first exogenous feeding, a critical period that shapes early survival rates in natural populations. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that such a small larval size is associated with high fecundity as a compensatory life-history strategy.

As juveniles transition toward reproductive maturity, body size at the onset of sexual maturation becomes a key demographic parameter. Field records indicate that the total length at puberty in Chanodichthys erythropterus is approximately 31.1 centimeters [Lp = approximately 31.1 centimeters], a value that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 212.6 grams [Wwp = 212.6 grams], estimated from the species length-weight relationship. This pubertal size is considerably smaller than the maximum attainable dimensions, reflecting a life-history pattern in which individuals become reproductively viable well before approaching their asymptotic growth phase. The onset of gonadal recrudescence and the first spawning event typically occur once this threshold body size is achieved, though local environmental conditions and prey availability can modulate the exact timing of reproductive activation. Comparative analysis with other large-bodied Asian cyprinids reveals that the relative length at puberty for this species—approximately thirty percent of ultimate length—is consistent with an iteroparous reproductive strategy, allowing multiple spawning seasons across an extended adult lifespan.

Reproductive output in Chanodichthys erythropterus is notably high, with females producing an estimated 526 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 526 eggs per spawning event] and completing approximately 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events per year] when maintained at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a rate inferred from the closely related species Chanodichthys dabryi, for which detailed captive spawning data are available. This per-event fecundity translates into a substantial clutch size during the spawning season. The reproductive investment per spawning event is considerable, reflecting the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and gamete production in a large-bodied iteroparous fish. At this thermal regime, the species exhibits a relatively compressed spawning period, with peak gamete release occurring over several weeks, after which females require a recovery interval before subsequent reproductive events.

The maximum lifespan documented for Chanodichthys erythropterus reaches ten years [am = ten years] at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a longevity that places this species among the longer-lived members of the genus. This decade-long lifespan provides multiple opportunities for reproduction across successive spawning seasons, consistent with the iteroparous life-history strategy inferred from the pubertal size parameters. Individuals attaining this maximum age typically exhibit the greatest body dimensions, with the ultimate wet weight recorded at 8298 grams [Wwi = 8298 grams] for the largest specimens sampled in gillnet surveys. The substantial increase in mass from the 0.0012 gram birth weight to over eight kilograms at senescence represents a mass gain exceeding six orders of magnitude, a growth trajectory that underscores the species' capacity for rapid juvenile development followed by a prolonged period of asymptotic growth during the adult phase. Mortality due to senescence is rarely observed directly in field populations, but scale annuli and otolith microchemistry analyses provide reliable age estimates confirming this decadal longevity.

The transition from a lecithotrophic larva weighing just over one milligram to an eight-kilogram adult predator requires a sustained high ingestion rate throughout the juvenile and sub-adult stages. The species achieves a maximum daily reproduction rate of 526 eggs per day [Ri = 526 eggs per day] at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a value that aligns with the high fecundity expected for a large-bodied cyprinid with pelagic eggs. The pubertal length of 31.1 centimeters [Lp = 31.1 centimeters] is reached within the first few years of life, allowing early initiation of reproductive activity, while the ultimate total length of 103 centimeters [Li = 103 centimeters] defines the upper boundary of the species' size spectrum. These parameters position Chanodichthys erythropterus as a high-fecundity, long-lived predator capable of dominating pelagic niches in its native eastern Asian drainages.
